content: Vitiligo, also known as leukoderma, is a chronic dermatological condition characterized by the loss of skin pigmentation, leading to the development of irregular, pale patches on the skin. The etiology of vitiligo is complex and not entirely understood, but it is believed to result from a combination of autoimmune, genetic, and environmental factors. It is the most prevalent depigmenting disorder globally, affecting approximately 1% of the population. The history of vitiligo dates back over 3,000 years, with descriptions of similar conditions found in ancient texts such as the Ebers Papyrus, the Atharva Veda, and even the Bible. The term vitiligo was first introduced by Celsus in the first century AD, and Moriz Kaposi later contributed to the understanding of its histopathological features. Clinically, vitiligo is classified into two subtypes: segmental vitiligo, which affects a single segment of the body (e.g., the face, arm, or leg), and non-segmental vitiligo, which involves multiple segments, such as both hands or both knees. The pathophysiology of vitiligo involves the destruction or loss of melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing skin pigment. Although the precise mechanism remains unclear, an autoimmune process is suspected in some cases. This hypothesis is supported by the higher prevalence of vitiligo in individuals with autoimmune disorders such as Addison's disease, hyperthyroidism, alopecia areata, and pernicious anemia. However, it is important to note that most individuals with vitiligo do not have any associated autoimmune conditions. Differentiating vitiligo from other hypopigmenting conditions is essential. Common differential diagnoses include pityriasis alba, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, tinea versicolor, halo nevus, tuberous sclerosis, and albinism. Epidemiologically, vitiligo affects both males and females equally, with a prevalence of 1% worldwide. Approximately half of all cases are diagnosed before the age of 20. Risk factors for developing vitiligo include a family history of the condition and the presence of autoimmune diseases. Individuals with a relative affected by vitiligo have an 18-fold increased risk of developing the disease, often with an earlier onset. The natural course of vitiligo is highly variable. Depigmentation may remain stable, progress to involve the entire body, or, in rare cases, remit spontaneously. However, spontaneous remission is uncommon. From a diagnostic perspective, vitiligo is typically asymptomatic and often presents during the second decade of life. It manifests as a gradual loss of pigmentation over time. Physical examination reveals irregular, pale patches of skin distributed in various patterns. Laboratory findings are generally unremarkable in vitiligo itself, but tests may be conducted to rule out associated conditions such as pernicious anemia, Addison's disease, or thyroid dysfunction. A skin biopsy, though not routinely performed, may reveal microscopic changes in the affected areas. Treatment options for vitiligo aim to achieve repigmentation of the affected areas. First-line therapies include potent topical corticosteroids, such as mometasone, and topical calcineurin inhibitors. Phototherapy has also been shown to be effective, particularly for generalized vitiligo. Combination therapy involving both topical calcineurin inhibitors and phototherapy has demonstrated superior efficacy in achieving repigmentation within a shorter timeframe compared to monotherapy. Support organizations play a crucial role in providing resources, education, and emotional support for individuals with vitiligo. Vitiligo Support International is the largest global organization dedicated to this condition, offering online forums, FAQs, and patient-referred doctor searches. The National Vitiligo Foundation (NVF) funds research, organizes workshops, and provides access to physician listings. The American Vitiligo Research Foundation (AVRF) focuses on raising awareness and supporting children and families affected by vitiligo, with an emphasis on finding a cure through non-animal testing methods. VITFriends, LLC, a support group based in the northeastern United States, provides encouragement and raises public awareness about vitiligo through its web-based community.
